reason: The central story of the broken circuit breaker switch and Buzz Aldrin using a felt-tip pen to rearm the engine is stated by only one source site (S6), so 10 multi-source claims cannot be produced for this specific narrative.
story: During the Apollo 11 mission in July 1969, Commander Neil Armstrong, Lunar Module Pilot Buzz Aldrin, and Command Module Pilot Michael Collins traveled to the Moon. While Collins remained in lunar orbit aboard Columbia, Armstrong and Aldrin landed the lunar module Eagle in the Sea of Tranquility. Armstrong became the first person to walk on the Moon, followed by Aldrin. Watched live by hundreds of millions of TV viewers on Earth, the moonwalkers spent about two and a half hours on the surface, deploying scientific instruments, collecting rock samples, raising an American flag, and speaking with President Richard Nixon via a phone call from the White House. Although popular history highlights Buzz Aldrin using a felt-tip pen to fix a broken circuit breaker switch before liftoff, only a single source in the set details that broken switch incident.
angle: An estimated 600 million people on Earth watched live as Apollo 11 astronauts made humanity's first steps on the lunar surface.

claims.claim: Apollo 11 landed humans on the Moon in July 1969.
The Apollo 11 crew consisted of Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin, and Michael Collins.
Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed on the lunar surface while Michael Collins remained in lunar orbit.
The Apollo 11 lunar module was named Eagle and the command module was named Columbia.
The lunar landing took place in the Sea of Tranquility.
Hundreds of millions of people on Earth watched the moonwalk live on television.
President Richard Nixon spoke to the moonwalking astronauts via radio-telephone from the White House.
Armstrong and Aldrin spent about two and a half hours exploring the lunar surface during their moonwalk.
The astronauts collected lunar rock and soil samples to bring back to Earth.
Armstrong and Aldrin erected an American flag and left a commemorative plaque on the lunar lander.
Neil Armstrong was the first human to step onto the Moon, followed shortly by Buzz Aldrin.
President John F. Kennedy set the national goal in May 1961 to land a man on the Moon and return him safely before the end of the decade.

disputed: The broken circuit breaker switch and felt-tip pen emergency repair (only documented in S6; leave out of multi-source script or attribute to single account).
Exact live television viewership figures (S1 estimates 600 million viewers, whereas S3 estimates 500 million viewers; script should state 'hundreds of millions').
Whether Neil Armstrong said 'one small step for man' or 'for a man' (audio transmission lacked the 'a', which Armstrong claimed was spoken or intended).
